title: A size fit gives 57 percent more mean squared error than a constant wait on six later Vela intervals
abstract: We test whether glitch size improves a forecast of the next large glitch in the Vela pulsar. We select fractional frequency steps of at least 10^-6 from a fixed Jodrell Bank catalog snapshot. We fit the first 12 resolved intervals and test the last six. The size fit gives an RMS error of 280 days; a constant wait gives 223 days. Mean squared error rises by 57.4 percent. A 95 percent pair-resampling range for the relative gain is -10.45 to 0.73, so the small sample does not establish a lasting loss or gain. Lower size cuts change the point result but do not give a resampling range above zero. A cut of 10^-7 recovers the published full-sample rank correlation of 0.585, yet gives only a 2.6 percent test gain. Timing error checks retain the main loss. Independent IAR timing supports the last event epoch, not the forecast relation. Catalog selection, unknown errors and shared timing fits remain limits. No new glitch or source is found. Code, selected source rows, exact provenance, controls, figures and offline steps are included.

display.caption: Early fit, six later forecasts, and sensitivity to the minimum glitch size. Error bars show 95 percent pair-resampling ranges with training refits. They are not physical confidence bounds.

citations.reason: Provides the shared data inventory and a catalog version audit. We use the same raw snapshot, but no code or derived rows.
Source catalog; exact frozen file hash and selected rows are included.
Version 2 reports a large-glitch size-to-next-wait correlation. We recover its rank statistic at its cut, then test an early fit on later intervals. We do not test its recovery models.
Prior multi-pulsar tests of size, wait and glitch classes.
Independent IAR timing supports the 2024 event epoch. It does not confirm our forecast result.
Small Vela glitches and timing-noise limits.
